steps.body: Back in third grade, you showed that 1/2 and 2/4 name the **same amount** — one bar cut into halves, the same bar cut into fourths, the same shaded area either way. Different cuts, same amount. That model is still the truth underneath everything in this chapter.
Cut it differently, cover the same amount.

widget.prompt: Build ANY fraction that covers exactly as much bar as 1/2.
widget.successFeedback: 2/4, 3/6, 4/8, 6/12 — all the same amount of bar. More pieces, smaller pieces, same total. That is what equivalent means, and the bar makes it impossible to doubt.
widget.lowFeedback: Your bar covers less than half. Either take more pieces or make them bigger.
widget.highFeedback: Your bar covers more than half. Take fewer pieces, or cut them smaller.

predict.prompt: You'll rebuild 1/2 using MORE pieces. To cover the same amount of bar, those pieces must be…
predict.reveal: More pieces of a smaller size can cover exactly the same amount — 3/6 uses six small pieces where 1/2 used one big one. Count up, size down, amount unchanged: that trade IS equivalence.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents equivalence recap.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for equivalence recap must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines equivalence recap.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

explanationVariants: Both name the same amount: 2 of 3 equal parts covers the same area as 4 of 6 equal parts of the same whole.
Picture the bar cut into thirds with 2 shaded, then the same bar cut into sixths with 4 shaded — same shaded area either way.

widget.prompt: Does 2/3 name the same amount as 4/6 (of the same whole)?

options.label: Yes — both cover the same shaded area
options.feedback: 2 of 3 parts and 4 of 6 parts shade the identical amount of the same whole.

options.label: No — 4/6 has bigger numbers, so it's more
options.feedback: Bigger-looking numbers don't mean more area — more cuts just means smaller pieces. 2/3 and 4/6 shade the same amount.

options.label: No — they use different bottoms, so they can't match
options.feedback: Different bottoms are exactly how equivalent fractions work — a different cut, same amount. 2/3 and 4/6 do match.

options.label: Can't tell without seeing a picture
options.feedback: You can check without drawing: 2 of 3 equal parts and 4 of 6 equal parts of the same whole are indeed the same amount.

steps.body: Look closely at 2/3 and 4/6. The bottom went from 3 to 6 — **doubled.** The top went from 2 to 4 — **also doubled.** That's not a coincidence. Every equivalent pair you've ever seen hides this same doubling, tripling, or other matching pattern.

explanationVariants: 1/4 to 3/12: the bottom went from 4 to 12 (×3), and the top went from 1 to 3 (×3) — the same multiplier both times.

widget.prompt: In 1/4 = 3/12, what happened to the top and bottom numbers?

options.label: Both were multiplied by 3
options.feedback: 1 × 3 = 3 and 4 × 3 = 12 — the exact same multiplier hit both numbers.

options.label: Only the bottom changed
options.feedback: The top changed too — 1 became 3. Both numbers were multiplied by 3.

options.label: 3 was added to both
options.feedback: Adding 3 to the top (1+3=4) doesn't match what's shown (it's 3, not 4). The real pattern is multiplying both by 3.

options.label: There's no real pattern — it's a coincidence
options.feedback: It's not a coincidence — every equivalent pair hides a matching multiplier. Here, both numbers were multiplied by 3.

widget.prompt: Sort each equivalent pair by what multiplier connects its top and bottom.
widget.missFeedback: Divide the new bottom by the old bottom to find the multiplier, then check it matches the top too.
widget.successFeedback: Every pair hides one shared multiplier connecting its top and bottom — ×2, ×3, or ×5 here.

explanationVariants: The bottom went from 5 to 20 — a ×4 jump. The top must follow the same ×4: 3 × 4 = 12.
Find the multiplier from the bottoms first (20 ÷ 5 = 4), then apply it to the top.

commonErrors.feedback: 15 would need a ×5 jump (3×5), but the bottom only jumped ×4 (5 to 20). Matching that: 3 × 4 = 12.
8 added 5 to the top instead of multiplying. The bottom's jump was ×4 (5→20); the top needs the same ×4: 3×4=12.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Find what the bottom was multiplied by (20 ÷ 5), then multiply the top by that same number.

hints: Apply that same ×3 to the top.
explanationVariants: The bottom jumped from 6 to 18 — a ×3 multiplier. Applying that to the top: 5 × 3 = 15.

commonErrors.feedback: 13 added 8 to the top (matching 6+12=18 style thinking). Equivalent fractions MULTIPLY, they don't add: 5 × 3 = 15.
18 just copied the new bottom. Find the multiplier first (18 ÷ 6 = 3), then apply it to the top: 5 × 3 = 15.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Find the multiplier from the bottoms (18 ÷ 6), then apply it to the top.

takeaways: Equivalent fractions still mean the exact same amount, cut differently — the G3 model never stops being true.
Every equivalent pair hides one shared multiplier connecting its top and bottom.
Finding that multiplier from the bottoms lets you predict the top, without drawing.
steps.teaser: next: WHY that shared multiplier always works — not just a pattern, but a reason.

concept.body: Quick rewind. Equivalent fractions share ONE multiplier between top and bottom. For 1/2 = 4/8: the bottom went 2→8 (×4), so the top must also go ×4: 1×4=4. Check the bottoms first, then match the top.

explanationVariants: The bottom jumped ×3 (3→9), so the top must also jump ×3: 2×3=6.

options.feedback: The bottom went ×3 (3→9); the top matches: 2×3=6.
8 added 6 to the top. Equivalent fractions multiply, they don't add: 2×3=6.
9 just copied the new bottom. Find the multiplier (9÷3=3), then apply it to the top: 2×3=6.
